question: What is God's name?
summary: The Hebrew Bible gives God several different "names" and in some cases insists that a particular one is THE name. Exodus 6:3 says God's name is Jehovah (YHWH), Exodus 3:14 gives "I AM THAT I AM," Isaiah 42:8 flatly claims "the LORD" is his name, Exodus 34:14 says his name is Jealous, Amos 5:27 says his name is the God of hosts, and Psalm 68:4 says his name is JAH. The contradiction is that multiple passages each claim to be stating THE divine name, and the names don't match.

reconcile.connective: Commentators treat the differing 'names' as one self-existent God variously rendered — JAH/I AM/Jehovah being the same name, and 'Jealous' an attribute, not a rival identity.

discrepancy.connective: The objection is pressed by Steve Wells in the Skeptic's Annotated Bible, who lists the passages that each declare THE divine name and notes they do not agree on one name.

pd_work.note: Gill treats this passage directly, identifying JAH as a contraction of Jehovah and equating it with the everlasting 'I AM' — the heart of the 'multiple names' objection harmonized at the verse.

excerpts.excerpt_text: God therefore told him His name, or, to speak more correctly, He explained the name יהוה, by which He had made Himself known to Abraham at the making of the covenant (Gen 15:7), in this way, אהיה אשׁר אהיה, "I am that I am," and designated Himself by this name as the absolute God of the fathers, acting with unfettered liberty and self-dependence.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly dissolves the I AM vs Jehovah tension: 'I am that I am' is presented as God's own explanation of the name Jehovah (יהוה), not a competing name. NOT shipped.
excerpts.source_note_text: When Moses had been thus emboldened by the assurance of divine assistance to undertake the mission, he inquired what he was to say, in case the people asked him for the name of the God of their fathers. The supposition that the people might ask the name of their fathers' God is not to be attributed to the fact, that as the Egyptians had separate names for their numerous deities, the Israelites also would want to know the name of their own God. For, apart from the circumstance that the name by which God had revealed Himself to the fathers cannot have vanished entirely from the memory of the people, and more especially of Moses, the mere knowledge of the name would not have been of much use to them. The question, "What is His name?" presupposed that the name expressed the nature and operations of God, and that God would manifest in deeds the nature expressed in His name. God therefore told him His name, or, to speak more correctly, He explained the name יהוה, by which He had made Himself known to Abraham at the making of the covenant (Gen 15:7), in this way, אהיה אשׁר אהיה, "I am that I am," and designated Himself by this name as the absolute God of the fathers, acting with unfettered liberty and self-dependence. This name precluded any comparison between the God of the Israelites and the deities of the Egyptians and other nations, and furnished Moses and his people with strong consolation in their affliction, and a powerful support to their confidence in the realization of His purposes of salvation as made known to the fathers. To establish them in this confidence, God added still further: "This is My name for ever, and My memorial unto all generations;" that is to say, God would even manifest Himself in the nature expressed by the name Jehovah, and by this He would have all generations both know and revere Him. שׁם, the name, expresses the objective manifestation of the divine nature; זבר, memorial, the subjective recognition of that nature on the part of men. דּר דּר, as in Exo 17:16 and Pro 27:24. The repetition of the same word suggests the idea of uninterrupted continuance and boundless duration (Ewald, 313a). The more usual expression is ודר ידר, Deu 32:7; Psa 10:6; Psa 33:11; or דּרים דּר, Psa 72:5; Psa 102:25; Isa 51:8.
